---
title: "Agent Skills 100: Telling the Agent How You Work"
---

## The global CLAUDE.md

Every time an agent starts a session, it reads a file called `CLAUDE.md` (or `AGENTS.md`) in the root of your repo. This is where you tell the agent about *this project* — how to build it, what the architecture looks like.

But there's also a **global** `CLAUDE.md` that lives in your home directory (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`). This one applies to *every* repo you work in. It's where you define your personal workflow — the phrases you use, what they mean, and what the agent should do when it hears them.

Think of it as training the agent to work the way you work.

## Set it up with a prompt

You don't need to write the file by hand. Start your agent and give it this prompt:

::: {.callout-note}
## Copy-paste this prompt into your agent

> Create `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` with my workflow preferences.
> Here is how I work:
>
> **"I am starting a new task"** means:
>
> 1. Create a GitHub issue for the task
> 2. Create a branch for the task
> 3. Work on the branch
>
> **"Task is done"** or **"Let's finish up the task"** means:
>
> 1. Open a PR
> 2. Merge the PR
> 3. Delete the branch
>
> Note: this assumes I'm working on my own. For collaborative work, I'll open the PR and assign a reviewer instead of merging.
>
> **"Get ready for clear"** means:
>
> 1. Close any loose ends (pending edits, uncommitted changes)
> 2. Review memories for outdated information and update them
> 3. Update the handoff note in `notes/`
> 4. Keep the handoff concise — move detailed info to separate files in `notes/` if it's getting long
> 5. Ask me what my next task will be when I return and put that in the handoff
>
> **"Initialize this repo"** means:
>
> 1. Add an open license if one is missing
> 2. Add a reuse statement to the repo
> 3. Check the README for basic reproducibility (instructions to run, dependencies listed, clear entry point)
>
> **Git rules:**
>
> - Never use destructive git actions: no `--force` pushes, no `git reset --hard`, no `git clean -f`, no deleting branches that haven't been merged
> - Always create new commits rather than amending
> - Ask before any action that could lose work
:::

The agent will create the file for you. Review it, tweak anything you want, and you're done.

Over time, add more shortcuts as you develop habits. The file grows with you.

## Where does it live?

The global `CLAUDE.md` lives at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` — in your home directory. But "home directory" means different things depending on where you're working.

### On JupyterHub (this clinic)

Your home directory is `/home/jovyan`. The file goes at:

```
/home/jovyan/.claude/CLAUDE.md
```

This persists across sessions on the same JupyterHub, but **it will be lost if the hub is rebuilt**. That's ok for learning. If you like what you've set up, save a copy somewhere permanent (see below).

### On a VM that gets torn down

Cloud VMs (like those from AWS, GCP, or Azure) often get rebuilt. Your `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` will disappear when that happens.

**Keep a backup.** The simplest approach: keep a copy in a repo you use across environments. When you spin up a new VM, copy it into place:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.claude
cp my-repo/dotfiles/CLAUDE.md ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
```

Or add it to your dotfiles if you manage those.

### On your personal computer

This is the most stable home. The file stays put until you change it:

- **macOS / Linux:** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
- **Windows (WSL):** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` inside your WSL home

This is where your global `CLAUDE.md` will eventually live long-term.

### The portable approach

If you work across multiple machines, keep your global `CLAUDE.md` in a small repo (or a gist) and copy it to each new environment. Some people keep a `dotfiles` repo for exactly this purpose.

The key habit: **when you change your global CLAUDE.md, update the backup too.**

## Global vs. project CLAUDE.md

| | Global (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) | Project (`./CLAUDE.md`) |
|---|---|---|
| **Applies to** | Every repo | This repo only |
| **Contains** | Your personal workflow and conventions | Project-specific build commands, architecture, coding style |
| **Examples** | "Starting a new task" means create issue + branch | "Run `quarto render` to build" |
| **Persists** | Tied to the machine / home directory | Committed to the repo, travels with it |

Both are loaded at session start. The project file adds context specific to the codebase. The global file carries your workflow everywhere.

## Customize it

The prompt above is a starting point. Here are some things you might add over time:

- **Code style preferences** — "Use snake_case for Python, camelCase for JavaScript"
- **Commit message format** — "Start commit messages with a verb: Add, Fix, Update, Remove"
- **Language** — "I work primarily in R and Python"
- **Review habits** — "Always show me a diff summary before committing"

Start simple. Add more when you find yourself repeating the same instruction across sessions.
